rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Objective 3 Setup 4 Gameplay 4.1 Rounds 4.2 Goals 4.2.1 Difficulty 4.3 Actions 4.3.1 Food 4.3.2 Bird Powers 5 End of Game Scoring Overview In Wingspan , each player will collect birds, each of which costs eggs and food to place. Each bird is worth points and has a special power. Make the right decisions and place the birds in the right environments to complete goals and earn points. Objective The player with the most points at the end wins. Setup Each player begins with: Five randomly dealt bird cards One of each food type ( seed , invertebrate , fruit , rodent , and fish ) Two bonus cards indicating a personal goal Before the game starts, each player chooses how many of their bird cards to keep. For each bird card kept, the player must discard one food. The more birds kept, the less food the player has at the start of the game. Before the game starts, the player must choose which of the two bonus cards to keep. You may only have one bonus card. Gameplay Rounds The game is played over four rounds. Round 1 has 8 turns per player Round 2 has 7 turns per player Round 3 has 6 turns per player Round 4 has 5 turns per player Goals Each round has a goal for all players shown on the goal board which are different for each round. Example goals: Birds in Wetlands Eggs on Birds with Bowl Nests Birds with Brown Powers Difficulty The competitive version of the goal board (green) has places for each player in order of rank (first gets the most points, second gets the second-most points, and so on). The less competitive version (blue) has each player earning up to 5 points for each of the given goal items earned. Each round ends when all players have made the given number of actions. At that point, the round goal is calculated, the face-up birds are replaced with new ones, and the "first player" privilege rotates to the player on the left. Actions On any given turn, a player may do one of the following: Name Description Habitat Play a Bird Place a bird card in its proper habitat (row) on the board. Birds must be placed from left to right. You must pay a food cost for the bird and an egg cost for the column. N/A Gain Food Collect food from the birdfeeder. Forest Lay Eggs Place eggs on bird cards. Grassland Draw Bird Cards Pick a bird card from the three face-up cards in the tray or draw a bird card from the deck. Wetland Food Food is found in the "birdfeeder" (dice tower), where five dice are rolled to determine what food is available. Each time a player takes a "Gain Food" action, they remove a die from the birdfeeder to gain the token shown on the die. When the birdfeeder is empty, all five dice are rerolled. If all dice in the birdfeeder show the same face, the player can choose to reroll all dice before taking any food. This can even be done if there is only 1 die left in the birdfeeder. Note: the dice with both a worm and wheat on the same die counts as its own unique face. You may use 2 of any food in place of 1 specific food. Bird Powers Nearly all birds have some text on the bottom of their card with some kind of ability or advantage. A skull icon next to the power indicates that bird is a predator. "When Activated" (brown) : When you take the Gain Food , Lay Eggs , or Draw Bird Cards actions, the action cube representing your turn is placed on the leftmost unoccupied space in the corresponding habitat. From there, the cube moves left onto each bird in the habitat. If the bird has a brown power, it activates. The "Play a Bird" action does not activate any of its benefits nor the benefits of other birds in that row. "Once Between Turns" (pink) : These powers trigger during the opponent's turn, but only once before your next turn. "When Played" (white) : These powers only activate once, when the bird is played. End of Game Scoring Scores are tallied from the following: Each bird's point value. Each card "tucked" under another bird card. Each food token "cached" on a bird card. Each egg on a bird card. Points earned from End-of-Round goals. Points from completing Bonus card objectives. The player who has the most points wins. In the case of a tie, the player with the most unused food tokens wins. If it's still a tie, tied players share the victory.

---

Wingspan is a competitive, medium-weight, card-driven, engine-building board game from Stonemaier Games. It's designed by Elizabeth Hargrave and features 180 birds illustrated by Natalia Rojas and Ana Maria Martinez.

You are bird enthusiasts—researchers, bird watchers, ornithologists, and collectors—seeking to discover and attract the best birds to your network of wildlife preserves. Each bird extends a chain of powerful combinations in one of your habitats (actions). These habitats  focus on several key aspects of growth:


     Gain food tokens via custom dice in a birdfeeder dice tower
     Lay eggs using egg miniatures in a variety of colors
     Draw from hundreds of unique bird cards and play them


The winner is the player with the most points after 4 rounds.

—description from the publisher

From the 7th printing on, the base game box includes Wingspan: Swift-Start Promo Pack.

[Rating: 1/10] Suffers from the same sort of problems that any one-big-draw-pile card game suffers from, and with no interaction between players, there really isn't much of a way to slow down someone who lucks into a run-away engine. The bonus cards are oftentimes distractions, sending players down suboptimal paths and offering little reward for doing so. That such a thoroughly mediocre game continues to ascend up the rankings, blowing past vastly superior games, lays bare how out of sync my tastes are with those of the wider audience on this site. It is produced beautifully, though.

But Wingspan's biggest problem is that it's a very mediocre game competing in a very crowded genre.   The scoring is so unfocused, that it's a bit of a mess. It's a multi-player solitaire when card tableaus have shown that they can be interactive. Indeed, there's not much reason to pay attention unless playing with competitive scoring. [Rating: 1/10] The worst multiplayer solitaire I’ve ever experienced. You are not engaged when it’s other players’ turn. You can not make any plans to speed up the game.  Random food with random birds.  Yeah, the components are pretty. The bird art and dice tower are nice, and it is somewhat educational. But that doesn’t make it a decent game.  BGG has lost its mind (and its credibility) over this plop of bird poop.

[Rating: 1/10] Huge deck of cards with no real way to mitigate luck of the draw.  I randomly lucked into a winning combo and then spammed it until the game thankfully ended.  The artwork is nice enough but the theme is a total disconnect like most nature themed games.  Everything about this game just rubs me up the wrong way and I'll never play it again. Twice was more than enough.

[Rating: 1/10] Finally played this. I enjoyed it. After one play I can tell that this would eventually become very "samey" and wear out it's welcome quickly. Nothing I desire to own. Dropped my rating to a 1 because of the normies voting this best innovate and best strategy game... HAHA!

[Rating: 1/10] Not very special. Everybody is just doing their own thing on their own tableau wich i do not care about. Lots of downtime.  The theme is also not interesting at all.  Cards to much randomness. All this makes it one of the most horrible games out there.

[Rating: 1/10] Average game, but makes a great centerpiece (shrinkwrapped of course) to show your friends you're part of the board game elite.

[Rating: 1/10] This game is boring. It's over produced, has little to no interaction. It's a luck based game where you might build an engine if the cards drawn allow it. When I played it I didn't care what anybody else was doing on their own board and that for me is bad design. I dont enjoy playing solo games and this is a solo game even when playing it with people. How this game has earned the kennerspiel des jahres is beyond me. Also its currently showing as the number 1 family game, which also is strange because I've never met a kid who would find this entertaining
